title: It's the Threat That Counts
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman summarizes a new working paper by Sarah Souders and Robert Bifulco that adds evidence for a claim he's made before: third-grade reading retention laws work primarily through the threat of retention, not the act of holding a child back. Studying Ohio's now-repealed policy, the authors compared students who scored just below the at-risk threshold in the fall against students who scored just above it, and found the flagged group scored higher on reading through at least 7th grade and on math through 6th grade - even though only about 3% of students were ever actually retained. The persistence of these gains for years after third grade, Aldeman argues, shows the effect isn't just short-run test-prep cramming. The mechanism the paper identifies is adult behavior change: students flagged as at-risk were more likely to get targeted literacy instruction, small-group or one-on-one tutoring, and specific help with vocabulary and fluency, and their families showed slightly better school attendance. The threat effect was strongest in places where schools themselves also faced accountability pressure tied to third-grade literacy rates, leading Aldeman to conclude that effective retention policy works by putting both students and the adults responsible for them on notice.
points: New research from Souders and Bifulco on Ohio's third-grade reading law finds that students merely flagged as at-risk of retention showed reading and math gains that persisted through at least 7th grade.

Retention rates stayed low and stable (about 3% actually retained) even though roughly a third of students were initially flagged, indicating the 'threat' itself — not the act of retention — is doing the work.

The mechanism is adult behavior change: flagged students were more likely to receive targeted literacy instruction, small-group or one-to-one tutoring, and specific help with vocabulary, fluency, and comprehension.

The threat effect was stronger in places where schools also faced their own accountability pressure for third-grade literacy rates, suggesting retention policy works best when it puts pressure on adults, not just students.
quotes: Instead, retention policies put adults on notice that a specific child needs help learning to read, and that causes the adults in that child's life to act differently.

There are two key points here. One is that the state has to issue a credible threat that a child will be held back if they fail to meet a clear and objective standard. And two is that there must be time to give that child the extra support they need to meet it.

They find that Ohio's third grade reading retention policy improved reading and math outcomes for students who were flagged as being at risk of being retained, and those academic gains lasted through at least 7th grade.
the persistence of positive effects through Grade 7 suggests that retention threat influenced more than short-run test-taking effort alone.

In fact, the authors find that adult behaviors changed in response. Students who were flagged as being at risk of being retained in the fall of their third grade year were more likely to receive targeted literacy instruction, participate in small group or one-to-one tutoring, and to receive special help on vocabulary, fluency, comprehension, or sight-word reading.

The Ohio results also suggest that the threat works best when adults face consequences of their own. The student retention rule was more effective when schools faced stronger accountability pressure for third grade literacy.
